title: FBC: Firebreak
summary: Leading UI/UX for a co-op multiplayer game, from the first wireframes in preproduction to post-launch support.

meta.label: Team
meta.value: Me and a UI artist, with 3 UI programmers

meta.label: Scope
meta.value: Information architecture, flows, HUD, menus, visual style, production planning

meta.label: Tools
meta.value: Figma, Claude AI, Photoshop, After Effects, JS/HTML/CSS, Jira, Confluence, pen and paper

hero.alt: FBC: Firebreak main menu inside a 3D environment

sections.heading: Role
body: I joined FBC: Firebreak in preproduction as the lead UI/UX designer. Firebreak is a three-player co-op shooter set in the world of Control.

A UI artist and I were the whole design side of the UI, working day to day with three UI programmers. Beyond the interface, I worked with art direction, the game director, game design, audio and VFX, and helped shape mission design and the gameplay loop.

sections.heading: Early playtests
body: Early playtests showed players couldn't read the game. Only 17% understood the mission objectives, and teammate visibility scored 1 out of 10.

Most issues came from a gameplay loop that felt confusing. The HUD made it worse: every new feature asked for its own on-screen feedback, and in a co-op fight it piled up until the game looked more complex than it was.

media.alt: In-game HUD during an anomaly interaction
media.caption: In-game HUD

sections.heading: Scope
body: A multiplayer game needs far more UI than its gameplay suggests: onboarding, a metagame, loadouts, cosmetics, matchmaking and parties, on top of the HUD. All of it had to ship together, designed by two people, on a schedule with little room for rework.

sections.heading: HUD
body: I argued against new on-screen feedback when players didn't need it. When they did, I looked for less intrusive ways to show it in the world, with VFX, animation or other diegetic cues. What stayed on screen had to be readable mid-fight.

media.alt: In-game HUD in a frost anomaly mission
media.caption: HUD in a live mission

sections.heading: Mission flow
body: For the confusing loop, I pushed for a simple mission tracker that always shows the player's next big goal. I also did a pass on the mission flow and cut the mission texts down, with less made-up jargon. Understanding of the objectives rose to 63%.
I didn't aim for 100%. Part of the fun is working out what needs to be done.

sections.heading: Teammate visibility
body: In a three-player game, you need to know where your teammates are at all times, with as little on screen as possible. I designed a colored silhouette for each player that shows through all terrain and meshes.
The visibility score rose to 7 out of 10, and 72% of players found it easy and intuitive, up from 11%.

sections.heading: 3D main menu
body: With the art director, I designed Remedy's first main menu set inside a 3D environment. Nobody at the studio had built one before, so the idea met early pushback. I worked out the technical approach that made it possible.

The menu shows the player's state in the game world with the actual game meshes. Each menu item has its own corner of the space, and the camera glides there on selection. The same setup supports seasonal and event environments.
sections.pull: Your loadout is the gear on the table in front of you.

media.alt: Loadout selection in the 3D menu space
media.caption: Loadout, shown on the table in the 3D menu

sections.heading: Matchmaking
body: I designed onboarding for the metagame and made matchmaking and the into-game flow modular, so players can browse and swap equipment and cosmetics while they wait in the queue.

sections.heading: Production planning
body: With two designers and that much UI, I also owned the UI plan. The producer ran the meetings, but the UI programming lead and I built the schedule together in Jira, sprint by sprint and screen by screen.
We started with screens that were safe to build early, and grouped screens that shared components so each piece was built once and reused.

sections.heading: User research
body: We tested the game with players throughout development, from 9 to 1,400 players per test.
Between 70% and 93% of players found the major UI features easy to use: the mission case board, where every match starts, plus upgrades and progression.
The share of players rating overall satisfaction 8 to 10 out of 10 rose from 31% to 51%. Part of that came from the added feedback and teammate visibility.

sections.heading: Launch
body: The game didn't find the commercial success we hoped for, and we didn't hit every goal we set for the craft team. The UI still shipped complete and working, on a very tight schedule.

sections.heading: What I'd do differently
body: This was my first time leading a project of this scale. More than once I had a gut feeling that a proposed feature or change wouldn't work, and let it through anyway. Next time I'd trust that instinct sooner, push back harder on requests from design and direction, and argue for the design I think works best.
